payload.rationale: No current data were supplied, so this is a base-rate judgment. Through 2025, US housing starts (SAAR) oscillated roughly between 1.25M and 1.45M, averaging near 1.33M, with single-family construction softening amid affordability constraints and elevated inventories of new homes, while volatile multifamily starts drove month-to-month swings. A 1.300M threshold sits near the center of that recent distribution, and contract thresholds of this kind are typically set close to prevailing expectations, so the outcome is close to a coin flip. Slight tilt below 50%: the underlying trend into late 2025 was gently downward (builders cutting starts, high completed-unsold inventory), and the first-print September figure is what settles, with typical month-to-month noise of ±5-8%. Reasons the estimate could be too high: if 2026 saw continued builder retrenchment or a weak labor market, starts could be running consistently in the 1.20-1.28M range, making 1.300M a meaningful hurdle. Reasons it could be too low: if mortgage rates fell materially in 2026 on Fed easing, starts could have rebounded above 1.35M, making 1.300M easy to clear; multifamily lumpiness also produces frequent upside spikes. Given genuine ignorance of 2026 monthly readings, I stay near even odds with a modest downward lean.
limitations: No 2026 housing starts data, mortgage rate levels, permit trends, or builder sentiment were supplied; all reasoning rests on pre-2026 background knowledge.
Uncertain whether the first-print September 2026 value on Trading Economics could be affected by release delays or revisions conventions.
Monthly starts are noisy (large standard errors), so even a well-known trend leaves substantial uncertainty around a single threshold.
